captions.albright:1:c2: Albright's father was a Czechoslovak diplomat in Belgrade, before the Second World War.
captions.albright:1:c3: When the Nazis invaded Czechoslovakia, her father escaped to Yugoslavia with his wife and baby.
captions.albright:1:c4: She remembered a little Serbian from her days in Belgrade as a child.
captions.albright:4:c1: Madeleine Albright arrived in the United States with her mother, her sister and her brother.
captions.albright:4:c2: Because of her father's job with the United Nations, she had the opportunity to come to America.
captions.albright:9:c1: As secretary of state, Madeleine Albright advocated for democracy and human rights.
captions.albright:10:c1: Madeleine Albright was a seven-time New York Times bestselling author: she is the author of Fascism: A Warning, and Hell and Other Destinations: A 21st-Century Memoir is a book by her.
captions.albright:15:r1: Here is the Old town square and Teyn Church, Prague, Czechoslovakia.

captions.albright:15:r3: This photograph by Gottscho-Schleisner shows a tourist lounge of the United States Lines.
captions.albright:15:r7: In this photograph by R. Michael Jenkins, of 1993, she is testifying in front of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during her confirmation hearing, holding a copy of the U.N. Charter.
captions.albright:15:r8: On this contact sheet of January 27, 1993: photographs of Vice President Gore swearing her in as Ambassador to the United Nations.
captions.albright:15:r9: Here she is with Ambassador Steinberg upon her arrival in Angola, in January 1996.
captions.albright:15:r10: This photograph by Bernard Gotfryd shows the U.N. Security Council Chamber, United Nations, New York. From 1993 to 1997, Albright served as the U.S. Permanent Representative to the United Nations.
captions.albright:15:r11: Here is the Oval Office: President Clinton speaking with Ambassador to the United Nations Madeleine Albright and others.

captions.albright:15:r14: At Camp Bonifas, Panmunjom, South Korea, on February 22, 1997, she shakes hands with American family members.
captions.albright:15:r15: In this photograph by Sharon Farmer, of October 15, 1998, she and President Clinton talk during the Wye River Plenary Session, near Queenstown, Maryland.
captions.albright:15:r16: Here she is at the Truman Library, Independence, Missouri, in March 1999, for the NATO Enlargement Ceremony.
captions.albright:15:r17: In this photograph by R. D. Ward, Secretary of Defense William Cohen, accompanied by her, speaks during the press conference at the Miguel Angel Hotel, Madrid, on July 8, 1997.
captions.albright:15:r19: This White House photograph shows President Barack Obama presenting the Presidential Medal of Freedom during the ceremony in the East Room, May 29, 2012.
captions.albright:15:r20: Funeral Service for Former Secretary of State Albright: a photograph by Freddie Everett, U.S. Department of State.
captions.albright:15:r21: On April 6, 2010, President Barack Obama greets her in the Family Theater of the White House.
captions.albright:15:r22: Here are photographs of the naturalization ceremony at the National Archives in Washington, D.C., on September 14, 2016, and of the rotunda, prepared for it. 59 years after she became a U.S. citizen, she was at the ceremony to make remarks.
captions.albright:ch:birth:opening: Madeleine Albright was born in Prague, Czechoslovakia, on May 15, 1937. Take a moment and look around.
captions.albright:ch:arriving:opening: In 1948, eleven years after she was born in Prague, Madeleine Albright steamed into New York Harbor, past the Statue of Liberty: her family immigrated to the United States. Take a moment and look around.
captions.albright:ch:citizen:opening: In 1957, nine years after her family immigrated to the United States, Madeleine Albright became a U.S. citizen. Take a moment and look around.
captions.albright:ch:big-work:opening: In 1993, Madeleine Albright, who became a U.S. citizen in 1957, was appointed Ambassador to the United Nations by President Clinton. Walk around, if you like.
captions.albright:ch:secretary:opening: On January 22, 1997, Madeleine Albright was confirmed as Secretary of State by the U.S. Senate. She was sworn in, in the Oval Office, on January 23, 1997, and Vice President Gore administered the oath of office. Take a moment and look around.
captions.albright:ch:history:opening: On July 8, 1997, Madeleine Albright talked to reporters in Madrid. At the NATO summit, the decision was to invite Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic. On July 14, 1997, she addressed the People of Prague at Obecni Dum. She was U.S. Secretary of State from 1997 to 2001. Have a look around.
captions.albright:ch:honoured:opening: Madeleine Albright was a recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom. On May 29, 2012, eleven years after her farewell remarks as Secretary of State, President Barack Obama presented it during a ceremony in the East Room of the White House. Take a moment and look around.
captions.albright:ch:legacy:opening: Madeleine Albright was a diplomat. Take a moment here.

captions.einstein:1:c5: Albert Einstein's Declaration of Intention is from 15 January 1936.
captions.einstein:1:c6: Look closely: a photograph of him is affixed to the Declaration of Intention.
captions.einstein:1:c8: His Petition for Naturalization has petition number 4009, assigned by the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey, Trenton.
captions.einstein:2:c2: During World War II, Albert Einstein was working as a consultant to the United States Government.
captions.einstein:2:c3: In his study at Princeton, N.J., he was doing research for the Bureau of Ordnance.
captions.einstein:2:c4: Nine letters were written by him to Lieutenant Stephen Brunauer, of the Research and Development Division, and the letters relate to his research with the Research and Development Division of the Navy, specifically underwater explosions and a proposed electromagnetic torpedo detonator.
captions.einstein:2:c6: Take his letter of June 18, 1943, to Lieutenant Stephen Brunauer. It discusses his idea of an electro-magnetic device that will automatically explode a torpedo as it passes underneath a ship.
captions.einstein:2:c7: In a letter of July 30, 1943, he reveals that he has come up with a mathematical simplification, to analyze the impact an underwater explosion would have on the hull of an armored ship.
captions.einstein:2:c8: Enclosed with his letter of August 13, 1943, to Lieutenant Stephen Brunauer, were signed copies of a contract and naturalization papers.
captions.einstein:2:c10: In this room, a corner recreates his study at Princeton, N.J., as two 1943 National Archives photographs show it.
captions.einstein:5:c1: On October 17, 1933, Prof. Albert Einstein was taken off the liner Westernland at Quarantine, and sped ashore by tug.
captions.einstein:5:c2: He arrived accompanied by Mrs. Einstein and Dr Walther Mayer, of Vienna, his assistant.
captions.einstein:5:c3: In October 1933, he came to Princeton by automobile, after he had debarked from the liner.
captions.einstein:5:c4: When he first came to Princeton in 1933, he lived at the address 2 Library Place.
captions.einstein:6:c2: Alexander Sachs delivered Einstein's letter to President Roosevelt on October 11, 1939.
captions.einstein:6:c5: His letter of November 29, 1947 includes the article “Atomic War or Peace,” which he authored.
captions.einstein:6:c6: In “Atomic War or Peace,” he discusses his opinion on the need of a supranational agreement for the regulation and use of nuclear weaponry.
captions.einstein:7:c8: Albert Einstein had a home study at 112 Mercer Street, in Princeton, New Jersey.
captions.einstein:7:c2: In 1976, the house at 112 Mercer Street, in Princeton, was designated a National Historic Landmark.
captions.einstein:7:c7: 112 Mercer Street remained his home until his death in 1955.
captions.einstein:7:c3: He died on April 18, 1955, at Princeton, New Jersey.
captions.einstein:9:c1: Albert Einstein received a Nobel Prize for Physics for his services to theoretical physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.

captions.einstein:ch:birth:opening: Albert Einstein was born in Ulm, Germany, on 14 March 1879. Take a moment and look around.
captions.einstein:ch:leaving:opening: Albert Einstein renounced his German citizenship in 1933, eleven years after he received his Nobel Prize. Take your time here.
captions.einstein:ch:arriving:opening: Albert Einstein immigrated to the United States. In October 1933, the same year he renounced his German citizenship, his party landed at the Battery, in New York. Have a look around.
captions.einstein:ch:citizen:opening: A year after his letter to the President, Albert Einstein received his certificate of American citizenship from Judge Phillip Forman, on October 1. Take a moment and look around.
captions.einstein:ch:big-work:opening: In September 1943, three years after he received his certificate of American citizenship, Albert Einstein was engaged in research work for the U.S. Navy, at Princeton, N.J. Walk around, if you like.
captions.einstein:ch:history:opening: In 1939, six years after he first came to Princeton, Albert Einstein signed a letter to President Roosevelt. Take your time here.
captions.einstein:ch:honoured:opening: Albert Einstein received a Nobel Prize for Physics. In Gottenberg [sic], Sweden, he delivered an address before a scientific body on his theory of relativity. Walk around, if you like.
captions.einstein:ch:legacy:opening: Albert Einstein pursued a unified field theory. Take a moment and look around.

captions.muir:1:c4: From Buffalo, Daniel Muir and his three children traveled across the Great Lakes to Milwaukee, and then overland to Kingston.
captions.muir:1:c2: In 1849, a ten-year-old, he left Scotland for the United States, in the company of his father, sister, and brother.
captions.muir:1:c3: The Muirs landed in New York City in 1849, and went by boat to Albany, and then across the Erie Canal to Buffalo.
captions.muir:1:c5: His father, Daniel Muir, named the farm Fountain Lake.
captions.muir:2:c3: In 1867, an accident nearly blinded John Muir.
captions.muir:3:c1: In 1880, on April 14, John Muir married Louie Wanda Strentzel.
captions.muir:3:c3: He co-founded the Sierra Club in 1892.
captions.muir:3:c5: In 1901, he published Our National Parks.
captions.muir:5:c1: John Muir and his family moved to their second Wisconsin farm, Hickory Hill.
captions.muir:5:c2: He assumed more and more of the work at the new farm, Hickory Hill.
captions.muir:5:c3: His cabin was by Yosemite Creek.
captions.muir:5:c4: At the Fountain Lake farm, he tried, for the first time, to preserve from human development a piece of land in its wild state.
captions.muir:5:c5: John Muir identified the Fountain Lake farm as the birthplace of his interest in preserving wilderness for its own sake.
captions.muir:7:n1: This is a room of the Hutchings hotel complex in Yosemite Valley, built round the trunk of an incense cedar. It is not John Muir's cabin.
captions.muir:9:c2: John Muir and other leading preservationists signed a petition that the Society for the Preservation of National Parks submitted to Congress.
captions.muir:9:c6: The petition signed by him urged Congress to defeat the Raker Bill, which called for a dam to be built across the Hetch Hetchy Valley.

captions.muir:13:r6: This is his illustration, from 1863, of a means to record time by use of a star, titled The star hand rising and setting with the sun all the year.
captions.muir:13:r8: Here is Muir’s signature in the Grand Register, photographed by Ralph H. Anderson.
captions.muir:13:r10: On this sheet is Pellaea ornithopus, from John Muir, 1875, in the Sierra Nevada, California.

captions.muir:13:r12: This photographic print of the Hetch Hetchy Valley, in the Sierra Nevada, is by Matt Ashby Wolfskill, 1911.
captions.muir:13:r15: Here are photographs of Muir’s Fountain Lake Home, from 1923. He lived continually at the Fountain Lake farm from 1849 to 1856.
captions.muir:13:r16: Here are photographs by Underwood & Underwood, of 1903: President Roosevelt on Glacier Point, Yosemite, and Theodore Roosevelt and John Muir on Glacier Point.
captions.muir:ch:birth:opening: John Muir was born on April 21, 1838, at 126 and 128 High Street, in Dunbar, Scotland. Take a moment and look around.
captions.muir:ch:arriving:opening: John Muir immigrated from Scotland to Wisconsin, to the Fountain Lake farm. Its farmhouse, made of white pine, was completed in October 1849, and in early November 1849 the rest of his family arrived from Scotland. Take a moment here.
captions.muir:ch:first-work:opening: In 1860, John Muir exhibited his inventions at the State Fair in Madison. He had a dormitory room in North Hall. Walk around, if you like.
captions.muir:ch:big-work:opening: John Muir first visited Yosemite in 1868, a year after the accident. In 1871, Emerson visited him in Yosemite. Walk around, if you like.
captions.muir:ch:study:opening: In 1890, ten years after he married Louie Wanda Strentzel, John Muir and the Muir family move into the big house in Martinez. Take a moment and look around.
captions.muir:ch:history:opening: In 1903, John Muir and President Theodore Roosevelt walked over to Glacier Point. That was two years after Muir published Our National Parks. Take a moment and look around.
captions.muir:ch:legacy:opening: In 1911, John Muir published My First Summer in the Sierra. He was a preservationist, and President of the California Branch of the Society for the Preservation of National Parks; here is the Hetch Hetchy Valley. Have a look around.

captions.naismith:1:c3: James Naismith attended McGill, and at McGill, Naismith had an appointment as instructor.

captions.naismith:11:c4: He was chapel director at the University of Kansas.
captions.naismith:11:c9: James Naismith died November 28, 1939, in Lawrence, Kansas, in his home just off the University of Kansas campus, at age 78.

captions.naismith:21:r7: Here is the Henderson daily dispatch of November 28, 1939: Man Who Invented Basketball Passes Of Heart Disease.

captions.naismith:21:r9: Here is the Evening star of November 5, 1961: Basketball First Day, first-day ceremonies for the 4-cent Basketball stamp honoring Dr. James Naismith.
captions.naismith:21:m1: In December 1891, Naismith invented basketball in Springfield.
